subject: biology
title: C2.1 Chemical signalling
welcome_lead: Today's adventure: C2.1 Chemical signalling — IB Diploma Programme Biology (guide first assessment 2025), topic C2.1.
meta_desc: IB DP Biology practice covering C2.1 Chemical signalling, guide topic C2.1.
final_note: You worked through C2.1 Chemical signalling — 14 guide statements.

concepts.def: A protein with a binding site whose shape and chemical properties are complementary to a specific signalling chemical. Binding of the signalling chemical is reversible and non-catalytic: the receptor changes conformation rather than changing the chemical, and this conformational change is what starts the cell's response. Receptors may be transmembrane proteins in the plasma membrane or intracellular proteins in the cytoplasm or nucleus.

The IB term for a signalling chemical that binds to the binding site of a receptor. Hormones, neurotransmitters, cytokines and autoinducers are all ligands for their receptors. A cell responds to a ligand only if it possesses a receptor with a binding site specific to that ligand, which is why the same chemical circulating through a whole body affects only particular target cells.

Cell signalling among bacteria in which each cell secretes a small signalling chemical (an autoinducer) into its surroundings. The concentration of autoinducer rises with population density; once it passes a threshold it binds to receptors in the cells and changes gene expression across the whole population, so behaviours that are only worthwhile at high density are switched on together.

The marine bacterium Vibrio fischeri lives free in seawater at low density, where it does not glow, and at very high density in the light organ of the Hawaiian bobtail squid, where it does. Each cell secretes an autoinducer (an acyl-homoserine lactone); when the population is dense enough for the autoinducer to reach its threshold concentration, it binds a receptor protein that promotes transcription of the lux genes, which encode luciferase, the enzyme that produces light.

A signalling chemical secreted by endocrine cells or glands into the blood, which transports it throughout the body. It acts on distant target cells that carry receptors for it, typically over minutes to hours and often on cells in several organs at once. Hormones are a functional category defined by how the chemical is released and delivered, not by its chemistry.

A signalling chemical released from the presynaptic membrane of a neuron into a synaptic gap, across which it diffuses to bind receptors on the postsynaptic cell within a millisecond. Its effect is localized to that synapse and short-lived, because it is rapidly broken down or reabsorbed. Some chemicals, such as noradrenaline, serve as neurotransmitters at synapses and as hormones when released into the blood.

A small protein signalling chemical secreted by cells, especially cells of the immune system, that mostly acts on nearby cells (or on the secreting cell itself) to coordinate responses such as inflammation, cell division and differentiation of immune cells. Cytokines are not produced by endocrine glands and are distinguished from hormones by their mainly local action and their cellular sources.

Calcium ions (Ca2+) are kept at a very low concentration in the cytoplasm by pumps. When channels open in the plasma membrane or in intracellular stores such as the endoplasmic reticulum, Ca2+ floods into the cytoplasm and binds to proteins that trigger rapid responses, including muscle contraction and release of neurotransmitter from a presynaptic neuron. Unlike the other categories, calcium ions are not synthesized by the cell and act as signals within the cell.

Hormones that are small molecules derived from a single amino acid, mostly tyrosine. Epinephrine (adrenaline) and noradrenaline are amines made from tyrosine; thyroxine is also tyrosine-derived. Being hydrophilic, epinephrine cannot cross the plasma membrane and binds to transmembrane receptors.

Hormones that are chains of amino acids, from short peptides to full proteins. Insulin is a protein hormone of 51 amino acids in two chains. Protein hormones are hydrophilic and so remain outside the cell, binding to transmembrane receptors in the plasma membrane.

Hormones that are lipids synthesized from cholesterol, with a characteristic four-ring carbon skeleton. Oestradiol, progesterone and testosterone are steroid hormones. Being hydrophobic, they pass through the phospholipid bilayer and bind intracellular receptors in the cytoplasm or nucleus.

Neurotransmitters are chemically diverse: amino acids (glutamate, GABA and glycine), peptides (such as endorphins), amines (such as dopamine, noradrenaline and serotonin) and a gas, which the guide lists as nitrous oxide (the gas that acts as a neurotransmitter is nitric oxide, NO). Acetylcholine, the transmitter at neuromuscular junctions, is a small molecule that fits none of these groups.

concepts.term: Reasons for chemical diversity of signalling chemicals
concepts.def: A body sends many different messages at the same time through the same blood and tissue fluid. Because each receptor binds only a ligand with a complementary shape, using chemically distinct signalling chemicals lets each message be read only by cells with the matching receptor, without cross-talk. Different chemistries also suit different jobs: hydrophobic steroids can enter cells and act on genes over hours, while small hydrophilic amines and amino acids act on surface receptors within seconds and are quickly removed.

Hormones are secreted into the blood and carried to every part of the body, so a hormone released in one place can act on cells in several distant organs simultaneously. The response develops over seconds to hours, and the hormone persists until it is removed by the liver or kidneys. Only cells carrying receptors for that hormone respond, so distribution is general but the effect is targeted.

A neurotransmitter is released into the synaptic gap, a space about 20 nm wide between the presynaptic and postsynaptic membranes, and diffuses across it in under a millisecond. Its effect is confined to the postsynaptic cell of that synapse and is ended quickly by enzymic breakdown or reuptake, so neurotransmitters give fast, precise, local effects, in contrast to the widespread, slower effects of hormones in the blood.

A receptor protein spanning the plasma membrane. Its membrane-spanning region is made of hydrophobic amino acids that sit among the hydrocarbon tails of the phospholipids, while the extracellular part carrying the ligand-binding site and the cytoplasmic part are made largely of hydrophilic amino acids. The ligand remains outside the cell; the signal, not the chemical, is passed across the membrane.

A receptor protein located in the cytoplasm or nucleus, with a largely hydrophilic surface so that it is soluble in the aqueous interior of the cell, and a hydrophobic pocket that binds its ligand. Its ligands are hydrophobic chemicals such as steroid hormones, which penetrate the phospholipid bilayer to reach it. Activated intracellular receptors typically act on DNA to change gene expression.

The sequence of responses within a cell that is set off when a ligand binds to a receptor. Binding changes the shape of the receptor, and this change is passed on through a series of molecular events (activation of proteins, production of second messengers, phosphorylation of enzymes) that ends in a response such as an enzyme becoming active, a channel opening or a gene being transcribed. The receptor initiates the pathway; the ligand itself usually never enters the cell.

A feature of many transduction pathways in which each activated component acts on many molecules of the next component, so that binding of a small number of ligand molecules produces a very large response. For example, one activated G protein activates an enzyme that makes many cAMP molecules, and each cAMP-activated kinase phosphorylates many enzyme molecules.

A transmembrane receptor at synapses and neuromuscular junctions that is itself an ion channel. When two acetylcholine molecules bind to sites on its extracellular part, the receptor changes shape and the channel through its centre opens, allowing positively charged ions (chiefly Na+) to diffuse into the cell down their concentration gradient. Acetylcholine itself stays outside the cell.

The membrane potential is the voltage across the plasma membrane, about -70 mV inside relative to outside in a resting neuron. Inflow of positively charged ions through opened acetylcholine receptor channels makes the inside less negative; this change is depolarization. If the depolarization reaches the threshold, it can trigger other changes such as an action potential in a neuron or contraction of a muscle fibre.

A transmembrane receptor with seven membrane-spanning helices. Binding of its ligand on the outside changes its shape, and the cytoplasmic part then activates a G protein attached to the inner face of the membrane. Humans have many hundreds of different GPCRs, responding to hormones, neurotransmitters, odours and light, and they are the targets of a large fraction of medicinal drugs.

A protein on the cytoplasmic face of the plasma membrane that binds guanine nucleotides. In its inactive state it holds GDP; an activated GPCR causes it to exchange GDP for GTP, on which an activated subunit separates and switches on an effector such as the enzyme adenylyl cyclase. The G protein hydrolyses its GTP back to GDP after a short time, which switches it off, so the signal is conveyed into the cell but not left on.

An amine hormone secreted by the adrenal glands during stress or exercise. It binds to G protein-coupled receptors in the plasma membrane of target cells such as liver cells, and its effects, including breakdown of glycogen to release glucose, are brought about via cAMP. Both names come from the hormone's production by the adrenal gland (Latin ad = at, ren = kidney; Greek epi = above, nephros = kidney) and remain in use in different parts of the world.

concepts.term: Cyclic AMP (cAMP) as a second messenger
concepts.def: A small molecule made from ATP by the membrane enzyme adenylyl cyclase when it is switched on by an activated G protein. cAMP diffuses through the cytoplasm and activates protein kinases that phosphorylate enzymes, for example switching on glycogen breakdown in a liver cell. It is called a second messenger because it carries the message of the first messenger, the hormone that remained outside the cell, to targets inside it.

A transmembrane receptor whose cytoplasmic domain is a kinase: when its ligand binds to the extracellular part, the receptor transfers phosphate groups from ATP onto tyrosine residues of its own cytoplasmic domain. These phosphorylated tyrosines start a sequence of reactions inside the cell. The insulin receptor is the IB example.

Insulin, a protein hormone, binds to the extracellular part of its receptor in the plasma membrane and stays outside the cell. Binding causes phosphorylation of tyrosine on the cytoplasmic side of the receptor, which triggers a sequence of reactions ending with vesicles that contain glucose transporter proteins moving to and fusing with the plasma membrane. The extra transporters increase the rate at which the cell takes up glucose from the blood.

An intracellular receptor for a steroid hormone such as oestradiol, progesterone or testosterone. The hormone diffuses through the plasma membrane and binds to a site on the receptor in the cytoplasm or nucleus, activating it. The activated hormone-receptor complex binds to specific DNA sequences near particular genes and promotes their transcription, so the response is a change in the proteins the cell makes and develops over minutes to hours.

concepts.term: Effect of oestradiol on GnRH-secreting cells
concepts.def: Oestradiol acts on cells in the hypothalamus that secrete gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH). At the moderate concentrations found through most of the cycle it inhibits GnRH secretion (negative feedback). When oestradiol rises to a high, sustained level as a follicle matures, its effect switches and it stimulates GnRH secretion (positive feedback), which drives the surge of luteinizing hormone that triggers ovulation.

concepts.term: Effect of progesterone on endometrial cells
concepts.def: Progesterone, secreted mainly after ovulation, acts on cells of the endometrium (the lining of the uterus). It maintains and thickens the endometrium, stimulates its glands to secrete and increases its blood supply, preparing it to receive an embryo. If progesterone secretion falls, the endometrium can no longer be maintained and is shed in menstruation.

Regulation in which the response to a stimulus acts to reduce or reverse that stimulus, so the system tends to return to a set level. Example: oestradiol, secreted by the ovary when GnRH has stimulated the pituitary to release gonadotropins, inhibits the hypothalamic cells that secrete GnRH, limiting further oestradiol production. Negative feedback counteracts change in either direction; it does not mean simply 'lowering'.

Regulation in which the response to a stimulus increases that stimulus, so the process is amplified until an end point is reached. Example: during birth, stretching of the cervix stimulates secretion of oxytocin, which strengthens uterine contractions, which stretch the cervix further; the loop ends with delivery. Positive feedback is a normal part of regulation used to drive a process rapidly to completion.

mcqs.q: Which statement correctly describes the relationship between a ligand and its receptor?
options: The ligand binds reversibly to a binding site on the receptor protein that is complementary to it, and the receptor changes shape.
The receptor's binding site converts the ligand into a product, in the way an enzyme's active site converts a substrate.
Any ligand reaching a cell binds to it, because every cell carries receptors for every signalling chemical in the body.
The ligand passes through a channel in the receptor into the cytoplasm, where it brings about the response directly.
mcqs.specStatementText: Receptors are proteins that bind one specific ligand
mcqs.explain: A receptor is a protein with a binding site specific to its ligand. Binding is reversible and does not alter the ligand; the conformational change in the receptor is what initiates the cell's response.
rationales: A receptor is a protein with a binding site specific to its ligand. Binding is reversible and does not alter the ligand; the conformational change in the receptor is what initiates the cell's response.
A student who transfers the enzyme model to receptors picks this. A receptor does not catalyse a change in its ligand; the ligand dissociates unchanged and it is the receptor that changes shape.

A student who thinks arrival of a chemical is what causes a response picks this. Cells carry receptors only for particular ligands, so a signalling chemical acts only on cells with a complementary binding site.
A student who pictures the signalling chemical doing the job itself picks this. Binding to the receptor sets off a sequence of responses inside the cell; the ligand itself usually never enters.

mcqs.q: Epinephrine (adrenaline) released into the blood reaches every organ. Liver cells respond to it by breaking down glycogen, but some other cell types show no response at all. What best explains this difference?
options: The blood carries epinephrine straight to the liver, so none reaches the other cell types.
Only the liver cells have receptor proteins whose binding sites are complementary to epinephrine.
Epinephrine can pass through the membrane of a liver cell but not through the membranes of the other cells.
Only liver cell receptors convert epinephrine into the product that triggers glycogen breakdown.
mcqs.specStatementText: Receptors are proteins that bind one specific ligand
mcqs.explain: All the cell types are exposed to the hormone, but a cell responds only if it possesses a receptor with a binding site specific to that ligand. Cells without the receptor are unaffected however much hormone reaches them.
rationales: A student who thinks the circulation routes a hormone to one target organ picks this. The stem states that the hormone reaches every organ; the difference lies in the cells, not in delivery.

All the cell types are exposed to the hormone, but a cell responds only if it possesses a receptor with a binding site specific to that ligand. Cells without the receptor are unaffected however much hormone reaches them.

A student who believes hormones enter cells to act picks this. Epinephrine is a hydrophilic amine that stays outside all cells and acts on a transmembrane receptor; membrane permeability is not the difference.

A student who treats the receptor as an enzyme acting on its ligand picks this. The receptor binds epinephrine reversibly and unchanged; it is the conformational change in the receptor, not a product made from the hormone, that starts the response.

mcqs.q: Vibrio fischeri produces light when packed at high density inside the light organ of a squid, but not when living at low density in seawater. Which explanation is correct?
options: The squid releases a chemical into its light organ that switches on the light-producing genes of the bacteria living there.
Each bacterium switches on its light-producing genes independently when its supply of nutrients in the light organ is high enough.
Autoinducer secreted by each cell only reaches the threshold that switches on the light-producing genes when cells are dense.
The autoinducer accumulating in the light organ is itself the substance that gives out light when it reaches high concentration.
mcqs.specStatementText: Bacteria count themselves with a shared secreted signal
mcqs.explain: This is quorum sensing. Every cell secretes autoinducer; its concentration tracks population density, and only above the threshold does it bind receptors and promote transcription of the genes for luciferase.
rationales: A student who looks outside the bacteria for the signal picks this. The signalling chemical is made and secreted by the bacteria themselves; the host provides the dense population, not the signal.
A student who assumes unicellular organisms act cell by cell picks this. The switch is coordinated across the population by a shared secreted signal, which is what makes it cell signalling.

This is quorum sensing. Every cell secretes autoinducer; its concentration tracks population density, and only above the threshold does it bind receptors and promote transcription of the genes for luciferase.

A student who thinks the signalling chemical performs the response itself picks this. The autoinducer is a ligand: it binds a receptor that promotes transcription of the lux genes, and the enzyme luciferase produces the light.

mcqs.q: What is quorum sensing in bacteria?
options: Bacteria counting neighbouring cells through direct contact between the surface proteins of their cell walls.
Bacteria of one species each responding on their own to the concentration of nutrients in their environment.
Bacteria secreting a chemical that itself gives out light once enough of it has built up around the cells.
A change in gene expression across a population when a secreted signal reaches a threshold concentration.
mcqs.specStatementText: Bacteria count themselves with a shared secreted signal
mcqs.explain: Each cell secretes an autoinducer; its concentration rises with population density, and above a threshold it binds receptors and alters gene expression in all the cells, as in bioluminescence in Vibrio fischeri.
rationales: A student who expects a head-count to need contact picks this. Density is sensed indirectly, through the concentration of a chemical that every cell secretes into the surroundings.
A student who thinks unicellular organisms do not signal to each other picks this. Quorum sensing is a response to a chemical made by the bacteria, coordinated across the population.

A student who thinks the signalling chemical performs the response picks this. The autoinducer is a ligand: it binds a receptor that promotes transcription of the lux genes, and the enzyme luciferase makes the light.

Each cell secretes an autoinducer; its concentration rises with population density, and above a threshold it binds receptors and alters gene expression in all the cells, as in bioluminescence in Vibrio fischeri.

mcqs.q: Which statement about the functional categories of signalling chemicals in animals is correct?
options: Cytokines are small proteins, secreted mainly by cells of the immune system, that act mostly on nearby cells.
Calcium ions are secreted by an endocrine gland into the blood and carried to distant target organs.
Cytokines are secreted by endocrine glands into the blood, from which they act on distant organs.
Neurotransmitters are carried in the blood from a neuron to the target cells of distant organs.
mcqs.specStatementText: Four functional categories of animal signalling chemicals
mcqs.explain: Cytokines are produced by ordinary cells rather than endocrine glands and coordinate local responses, especially among immune cells; this local action distinguishes them from hormones.
rationales: Cytokines are produced by ordinary cells rather than endocrine glands and coordinate local responses, especially among immune cells; this local action distinguishes them from hormones.
A student who pictures calcium as a substance carried in blood picks this. Calcium ions signal within cells: a rise in cytoplasmic Ca2+ when channels open triggers responses such as contraction.
A student who files every new chemical messenger as a hormone picks this. Cytokines come from cells such as immune cells, not glands, and act mainly locally.
A student who thinks all chemical messengers travel in blood picks this. A neurotransmitter diffuses across a synaptic gap of about 20 nm to the adjacent cell and acts locally.

mcqs.q: Noradrenaline is released by sympathetic neurons into synaptic gaps and is also released by the adrenal glands into the blood. What does this show about the categories hormone and neurotransmitter?
options: Noradrenaline must be a hormone rather than a neurotransmitter, since a chemical belongs to only one category.
They are functional categories, so one chemical can belong to either depending on how it is released and reaches its target.
In both cases the noradrenaline is carried in the blood to the cells it acts on, so the two categories cannot be distinguished.
The blood carries adrenal noradrenaline only to the same cells that the sympathetic neurons already reach.
mcqs.specStatementText: Four functional categories of animal signalling chemicals
mcqs.explain: A hormone is defined by transport in the blood to distant cells and a neurotransmitter by diffusion across a synaptic gap. The definitions are about delivery, not chemistry, so noradrenaline is a neurotransmitter at synapses and a hormone in the blood.
rationales: A student who treats the categories as chemical classes picks this. The categories are functional, and the stem shows the same substance being used in both ways.

A hormone is defined by transport in the blood to distant cells and a neurotransmitter by diffusion across a synaptic gap. The definitions are about delivery, not chemistry, so noradrenaline is a neurotransmitter at synapses and a hormone in the blood.

A student who thinks neurotransmitters travel in blood picks this. At a synapse noradrenaline diffuses across the synaptic gap and never enters the blood; the two routes are what separate the categories.
A student who thinks the blood delivers a hormone to a single target picks this. Noradrenaline in the blood reaches every organ and acts on all cells that carry its receptors.

mcqs.q: To which chemical groups do the hormones epinephrine, insulin and testosterone belong?
options: Epinephrine, insulin and testosterone are all proteins made of amino acids.
Epinephrine is a steroid, insulin is a protein and testosterone is a steroid as well.
Epinephrine is an amine, insulin is a protein and testosterone is a steroid.
Epinephrine is an amine, insulin is a protein and testosterone is a small protein.
mcqs.specStatementText: Signalling chemicals are chemically diverse, and that is useful
mcqs.explain: These are the three chemical groups of hormones the guide requires: amines derived from an amino acid (epinephrine), proteins (insulin) and steroids derived from cholesterol (testosterone).
rationales: A student who generalises from insulin picks this. Only insulin is a protein; epinephrine is a small amine and testosterone is a lipid.
A student who links epinephrine to the adrenal gland's steroids picks this. Epinephrine is an amine made from tyrosine, not a steroid from cholesterol.
These are the three chemical groups of hormones the guide requires: amines derived from an amino acid (epinephrine), proteins (insulin) and steroids derived from cholesterol (testosterone).
A student who thinks of steroids as protein-builders and hence as proteins picks this. Testosterone is a steroid, a lipid with a four-ring carbon skeleton.

mcqs.q: Why is it advantageous for animals to use a wide range of chemically different substances as signalling chemicals rather than a single one?
options: The chemical nature of a signal does not matter, because a receptor recognises the message rather than the shape of the molecule.
Hormones must be large molecules and neurotransmitters small ones, so each category needs its own chemical class.
Each receptor breaks its ligand down into a different product, so a different chemical is needed for every product required.
Many messages can travel in the same fluid at once, each read only by cells with the matching receptor.
mcqs.specStatementText: Signalling chemicals are chemically diverse, and that is useful
mcqs.explain: Receptor binding sites are specific, so chemically distinct ligands let many signals coexist in the blood and tissue fluid without cross-talk. Different chemistries also suit different speeds, durations and receptor locations.
rationales: A student who separates the message from the molecule picks this. Specificity comes from the complementary shape and chemistry of ligand and binding site, so distinct messages need chemically distinct ligands.
A student who treats the functional categories as chemical classes picks this. Both categories contain small amines and larger peptides; chemistry does not define the category.
A student who treats receptors as enzymes acting on ligands picks this. Receptors do not convert their ligands; the response comes from a transduction pathway inside the cell.

Receptor binding sites are specific, so chemically distinct ligands let many signals coexist in the blood and tissue fluid without cross-talk. Different chemistries also suit different speeds, durations and receptor locations.

mcqs.q: Chemical X is released from one cell, diffuses about 20 nm and acts on a single adjacent cell within a millisecond before being broken down. Chemical Y is released into the blood and, over several minutes, acts on cells in the liver, heart and skeletal muscle. Which statement is correct?
options: X is a neurotransmitter acting locally across a synaptic gap, and Y is a hormone acting at a distance after transport in the blood.
Both are hormones, because a chemical released from a cell to act on another cell has to travel through the blood.
Y is a neurotransmitter, because a hormone would be delivered by the blood to a single target organ rather than to several.
X acts faster because it enters the target cell and carries out the response itself, whereas Y has to bind a receptor.
mcqs.specStatementText: Hormones act far away; neurotransmitters act next door
mcqs.explain: The 20 nm diffusion distance, millisecond timing and single target cell are the marks of a neurotransmitter; transport in the blood and effects on cells in several organs over minutes are the marks of a hormone.
rationales: The 20 nm diffusion distance, millisecond timing and single target cell are the marks of a neurotransmitter; transport in the blood and effects on cells in several organs over minutes are the marks of a hormone.
A student who thinks every chemical messenger uses the blood picks this. X crosses a synaptic gap by diffusion and never enters the blood.
A student who thinks the blood routes a hormone to a single organ picks this. The blood distributes a hormone everywhere, so acting on several organs is typical of a hormone, not evidence against it.

A student who pictures the signalling chemical doing the job itself picks this. X binds a receptor on the adjacent cell; its speed comes from the tiny distance it diffuses, not from entering the cell.

mcqs.q: Insulin is a hydrophilic protein and oestradiol is a hydrophobic steroid. Where are their receptors, and do the hormones enter their target cells?
options: Both stay outside and bind receptors on the cell surface, because all receptors are proteins embedded in the plasma membrane.
Insulin stays outside and binds a transmembrane receptor; oestradiol passes through the membrane and binds an intracellular receptor.
Both enter the cell, because a signalling chemical has to reach the cytoplasm in order to bring about any response at all.
Insulin stays outside and binds a transmembrane receptor; oestradiol is carried through the membrane by a transport protein to a receptor inside.
mcqs.specStatementText: Surface receptors for ligands that stay out; internal receptors for ligands that get in
mcqs.explain: A hydrophilic protein cannot cross the phospholipid bilayer, so its receptor spans the plasma membrane and the ligand remains outside. A hydrophobic steroid dissolves through the bilayer to reach a receptor in the cytoplasm or nucleus.
rationales: A student who has only seen surface receptors picks this. Steroid hormones penetrate the cell and bind intracellular receptors, which then act on DNA.

A hydrophilic protein cannot cross the phospholipid bilayer, so its receptor spans the plasma membrane and the ligand remains outside. A hydrophobic steroid dissolves through the bilayer to reach a receptor in the cytoplasm or nucleus.
A student who believes hormones enter cells to act picks this. Insulin, being a hydrophilic protein, cannot cross the membrane; its signal is passed inside by the receptor.

A student who thinks hydrophobic molecules are excluded by the membrane picks this. Steroids dissolve through the hydrophobic core of the bilayer by simple diffusion; no carrier is needed to reach the intracellular receptor.

mcqs.q: The amino acid sequence of a newly discovered receptor shows seven stretches of about 20 mostly hydrophobic amino acids, separated by hydrophilic regions. Its ligand, a short peptide, binds to one of the hydrophilic regions. What can be concluded?
options: It is an intracellular receptor, because a protein containing hydrophilic regions could not remain embedded within the lipid bilayer.
It is a transmembrane receptor whose ligand enters the cell through the hydrophilic regions to act in the cytoplasm.
It is a transmembrane receptor: the hydrophobic stretches span the bilayer and the ligand binds a hydrophilic part outside.
The seven hydrophobic stretches form a channel through which the ligand passes into the cell to activate a G protein on the inner face.
mcqs.specStatementText: Surface receptors for ligands that stay out; internal receptors for ligands that get in
mcqs.explain: Membrane-spanning regions are made of hydrophobic amino acids that sit among the phospholipid tails, while the parts exposed to water on each side are hydrophilic. A ligand binding to a hydrophilic region on the outer face remains outside the cell.
rationales: A student who expects a membrane protein to be hydrophobic throughout picks this. Transmembrane receptors are hydrophobic only where they cross the bilayer and hydrophilic where they project into watery surroundings.
A student who thinks the signalling chemical must get in picks this. A ligand that binds a transmembrane receptor stays outside; the receptor's change of shape carries the signal across.

Membrane-spanning regions are made of hydrophobic amino acids that sit among the phospholipid tails, while the parts exposed to water on each side are hydrophilic. A ligand binding to a hydrophilic region on the outer face remains outside the cell.

A student who thinks the ligand travels through a G protein-coupled receptor picks this. Seven membrane-spanning helices are typical of a GPCR, but nothing passes through it; a conformational change activates the G protein.

mcqs.q: What is meant by the initiation of a signal transduction pathway by a receptor?
options: The ligand enters the cytoplasm after binding and itself performs the response inside the cell.
The receptor converts the ligand into a product, and the product produced is the cell's response.
The receptor makes exactly one molecule of response product for each ligand molecule that binds to it.
Ligand binding changes the receptor's shape, setting off a sequence of responses in the cell.
mcqs.specStatementText: Receptor activation starts a chain of events inside the cell
mcqs.explain: The receptor initiates the pathway: the conformational change caused by binding is passed on through a series of intracellular events, such as activation of proteins and production of second messengers, that ends in the response.
rationales: A student who pictures the signalling chemical as the agent of the response picks this. The response is carried out by components of the pathway inside the cell; the ligand usually stays outside.
A student who treats the receptor as an enzyme acting on its ligand picks this. The ligand is not changed; the receptor changes shape and the response arises from the cascade this triggers.
A student who reasons one-to-one, as in a chemical equation, picks this. Transduction pathways amplify the signal, so one bound ligand can lead to a very large response.

The receptor initiates the pathway: the conformational change caused by binding is passed on through a series of intracellular events, such as activation of proteins and production of second messengers, that ends in the response.

mcqs.q: Acetylcholine released at a neuromuscular junction binds to acetylcholine receptors in the membrane of a muscle fibre. What happens next?
options: An ion channel in the receptor opens, positive ions diffuse into the fibre and the membrane potential becomes less negative.
Acetylcholine passes through the channel in the receptor, carrying its positive charge into the fibre with it.
An ion channel in the receptor opens, positively charged ions leave the fibre and the inside becomes more negative.
Acetylcholine enters the fibre and binds directly to the contractile proteins, causing them to shorten at once.
mcqs.specStatementText: Neurotransmitter receptors open channels and change the voltage
mcqs.explain: The acetylcholine receptor is a ligand-gated ion channel. Binding opens the channel, Na+ diffuses in down its concentration gradient, and the resulting depolarization may trigger contraction.
rationales: The acetylcholine receptor is a ligand-gated ion channel. Binding opens the channel, Na+ diffuses in down its concentration gradient, and the resulting depolarization may trigger contraction.
A student who thinks the channel is for the ligand picks this. Acetylcholine stays bound on the outside; it is Na+ that diffuses through the opened channel.
A student who has the direction of ion movement or the sign convention reversed picks this. Na+ is concentrated outside, so it enters, and inflow of positive charge depolarizes the membrane.
A student who thinks the signalling chemical performs the response itself picks this. Contraction follows a change in membrane potential set off by the receptor; acetylcholine never enters the fibre.

mcqs.q: A muscle fibre has a resting membrane potential of -70 mV. When acetylcholine is applied, the potential changes to -50 mV within 1 ms. If sodium ions are first removed from the fluid outside the fibre, acetylcholine still binds but the potential stays at -70 mV. What do these results show?
options: The change to -50 mV is caused by positive ions leaving the fibre, a movement that needs sodium outside to draw them out.
The change to -50 mV is caused by Na+ diffusing into the fibre through channels opened by acetylcholine binding.
Acetylcholine itself enters through the channel, but it can only do so if it is carried in by sodium ions.
Acetylcholine binding activates a G protein that makes cAMP, and the cAMP needs sodium to raise the potential.
mcqs.specStatementText: Neurotransmitter receptors open channels and change the voltage
mcqs.explain: The potential becomes less negative (depolarization) only when Na+ is available outside, so inflow of these positively charged ions through the opened receptor channels is what changes the voltage across the membrane.
rationales: A student who reverses the direction of ion movement picks this. Loss of positive ions would make the inside more negative, not less; the shift towards zero shows positive charge entering.

The potential becomes less negative (depolarization) only when Na+ is available outside, so inflow of these positively charged ions through the opened receptor channels is what changes the voltage across the membrane.
A student who thinks the ligand passes through its receptor picks this. Acetylcholine binds and stays outside; the dependence on external Na+ shows it is Na+ that moves in.
A student who applies one mechanism to every receptor picks this. The acetylcholine receptor is itself an ion channel; no G protein or second messenger is involved in this millisecond response.

mcqs.q: How does a G protein-coupled receptor convey a signal into a cell?
options: The ligand passes through a channel in the receptor and binds directly to the G protein, which lies in the cytoplasm just beneath the membrane.
The G protein is released from the membrane into the blood as a second messenger that carries the signal to neighbouring cells of the tissue.
Binding of the ligand outside changes the receptor's shape, activating a G protein on the inner face, which then activates an effector.
The activated G protein converts ATP into cAMP directly, and the cAMP then brings about the response inside the cell.
mcqs.specStatementText: Some receptors pass the signal to a G protein
mcqs.explain: The receptor spans the membrane; the conformational change caused by binding is transmitted to its cytoplasmic part, which activates the G protein. The activated G protein switches on an effector such as adenylyl cyclase. Humans have many hundreds of such receptors.
rationales: A student who thinks the ligand travels through the receptor to its target picks this. Nothing passes through a GPCR; the signal crosses as a change in protein shape.
A student who reads 'second messenger' as another circulating hormone picks this. The G protein stays on the inner face of the membrane, and second messengers such as cAMP act within the cell.

The receptor spans the membrane; the conformational change caused by binding is transmitted to its cytoplasmic part, which activates the G protein. The activated G protein switches on an effector such as adenylyl cyclase. Humans have many hundreds of such receptors.
A student who collapses the pathway picks this. The G protein activates the enzyme adenylyl cyclase, and it is this enzyme that converts ATP into cAMP.

mcqs.q: A hormone binds to a G protein-coupled receptor on cells, and an enzyme inside the cells becomes active. A toxin that locks the G protein in its inactive form is added. The hormone still binds to the receptor, but the enzyme is no longer activated. What does this show?
options: The toxin has blocked the channel in the receptor through which the hormone normally enters the cell.
The hormone has to reach the enzyme itself to activate it, and the toxin prevents the hormone from entering.
The G protein converts the bound hormone into cAMP, so without it no second messenger can be formed.
The G protein is needed to convey the signal from the occupied receptor to the enzyme inside.
mcqs.specStatementText: Some receptors pass the signal to a G protein
mcqs.explain: Binding is unaffected, so the receptor is intact; the response fails only because the G protein cannot be activated. This isolates the G protein's role as the link between receptor and effector.
rationales: A student who thinks the ligand goes through the receptor picks this. The hormone never enters; it binds outside and the stem shows binding is unaffected.

A student who pictures the hormone performing the response picks this. The hormone acts only on the receptor; the enzyme is activated through the intracellular pathway, which the toxin interrupts at the G protein.

A student who gives the G protein the enzyme's job picks this. cAMP is made from ATP by adenylyl cyclase, and the hormone is never converted into anything; the G protein's role is to activate the effector.
Binding is unaffected, so the receptor is intact; the response fails only because the G protein cannot be activated. This isolates the G protein's role as the link between receptor and effector.

mcqs.q: Which sequence correctly describes the events after epinephrine (adrenaline) binds to its receptor on a liver cell?
options: A G protein is activated, adenylyl cyclase converts ATP to cAMP, and cAMP activates kinases that switch on glycogen breakdown.
Epinephrine enters the liver cell and directly activates the enzymes that break down glycogen into glucose.
cAMP is released from the liver cell into the blood as a second messenger that acts on other liver cells.
The activated G protein converts ATP into cAMP, and the cAMP then breaks glycogen down directly into glucose.
mcqs.specStatementText: Epinephrine acts through a G protein and cAMP
mcqs.explain: The epinephrine receptor is a G protein-coupled receptor. The activated G protein switches on adenylyl cyclase, the second messenger cAMP activates protein kinases, and the phosphorylated enzymes break down glycogen to release glucose.
rationales: The epinephrine receptor is a G protein-coupled receptor. The activated G protein switches on adenylyl cyclase, the second messenger cAMP activates protein kinases, and the phosphorylated enzymes break down glycogen to release glucose.
A student who thinks hormones enter their target cells picks this. Epinephrine is hydrophilic and stays outside; the message is carried inside by the G protein and cAMP.
A student who reads 'second messenger' as a second hormone picks this. cAMP is made and acts within the cell; it is called a second messenger because it relays the hormone's message inside the cell.
A student who collapses the pathway picks this. Adenylyl cyclase makes cAMP, and cAMP acts by activating kinases; it does not hydrolyse glycogen itself.

mcqs.q: Binding of a few molecules of epinephrine to receptors on a liver cell leads to the release of many thousands of glucose molecules. Which feature of the signalling pathway explains this?
options: The receptor converts each epinephrine molecule it binds into an active enzyme, and that enzyme releases the glucose.
Each activated G protein, adenylyl cyclase and kinase acts on many molecules of the next component, amplifying the signal.
The pathway cannot amplify the signal, so the cell must in fact have bound many thousands of epinephrine molecules at the same time.
cAMP leaves the cell and recruits neighbouring liver cells, which together release the large amount of glucose.
mcqs.specStatementText: Epinephrine acts through a G protein and cAMP
mcqs.explain: One receptor can activate several G proteins, each adenylyl cyclase makes many cAMP molecules, and each activated kinase phosphorylates many enzyme molecules, so a small number of ligand molecules produces a very large response.
rationales: A student who treats the receptor as an enzyme acting on its ligand picks this. Epinephrine is not converted into anything; the amplification comes from each component of the intracellular cascade acting on many molecules of the next.

One receptor can activate several G proteins, each adenylyl cyclase makes many cAMP molecules, and each activated kinase phosphorylates many enzyme molecules, so a small number of ligand molecules produces a very large response.
A student who reasons one ligand to one product picks this. Signal transduction cascades amplify at several steps, which is exactly why hormones are effective at very low concentrations.
A student who thinks the second messenger is exported picks this. cAMP acts inside the cell that made it; the amplification happens within a single cell's cascade.

mcqs.q: Which sequence correctly describes how insulin increases glucose uptake by a muscle cell?
options: Insulin enters the cell bound to glucose and releases it in the cytoplasm; the empty insulin then returns to the blood to collect more glucose.
Insulin binds the receptor, which phosphorylates free tyrosine in the cytoplasm; the phosphorylated tyrosine then binds glucose molecules and pulls them into the cell.
Insulin binds the receptor outside; tyrosines on its cytoplasmic part are phosphorylated; a cascade moves vesicles with glucose transporters to the membrane.
Insulin binds the receptor; the signal activates transcription of the transporter genes, and the newly synthesized glucose transporters are then inserted into the membrane.
mcqs.specStatementText: Insulin's receptor phosphorylates itself, and glucose transporters arrive
mcqs.explain: The insulin receptor has tyrosine kinase activity: binding of the hormone outside causes phosphorylation of tyrosine inside the cell, and the resulting cascade ends with vesicles containing glucose transporters fusing with the plasma membrane, so more glucose enters.
rationales: A student who imagines insulin as a carrier for glucose picks this. Insulin is a protein that cannot cross the membrane; glucose enters through transporter proteins that the insulin signal adds to the membrane.

A student who reads 'phosphorylation of tyrosine' as the free amino acid picks this. The tyrosines phosphorylated are residues within the receptor and other proteins, and glucose enters through transporters, not bound to tyrosine.

The insulin receptor has tyrosine kinase activity: binding of the hormone outside causes phosphorylation of tyrosine inside the cell, and the resulting cascade ends with vesicles containing glucose transporters fusing with the plasma membrane, so more glucose enters.

A student who assumes more protein in the membrane requires new gene expression picks this. The transporters already exist in vesicles; the response is their movement to the plasma membrane, which is why it is fast.

mcqs.q: How does a steroid hormone such as testosterone change the expression of genes in a target cell?
options: It diffuses through the membrane into the nucleus and binds directly to the DNA at the start of the genes it switches on.
It binds a receptor in the plasma membrane, and this receptor then detaches and travels to the nucleus to bind the DNA.
It is pumped across the membrane by a transport protein, since steroids cannot cross the bilayer, and then activates a receptor inside.
It enters the cell and activates a receptor inside it, which binds specific DNA sequences to promote transcription.
mcqs.specStatementText: Steroid hormones enter the cell and switch on genes
mcqs.explain: Steroids are hydrophobic and penetrate the cell. Binding to a site on the receptor activates it; the hormone-receptor complex binds specific DNA sequences and promotes transcription of particular genes.
rationales: A student who leaves out the receptor picks this. The hormone has no DNA-binding ability; it is the activated receptor protein that recognises specific DNA sequences.
A student who places every receptor on the cell surface picks this. Steroid receptors are intracellular, in the cytoplasm or nucleus, and the hormone enters the cell to reach them.
A student who thinks hydrophobic molecules are excluded by the membrane picks this. Steroids dissolve through the hydrophobic core of the bilayer by simple diffusion; no transport protein is needed.

Steroids are hydrophobic and penetrate the cell. Binding to a site on the receptor activates it; the hormone-receptor complex binds specific DNA sequences and promotes transcription of particular genes.

mcqs.q: Cells respond to testosterone only after about 30 minutes, and the response is abolished by a drug that blocks transcription. The same cells respond to epinephrine within seconds, and this response is unaffected by the drug. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: Testosterone acts via an intracellular receptor that promotes transcription, so its effect needs new mRNA; epinephrine acts on enzymes already present.
The drug prevents testosterone itself from binding to the DNA of the target genes, which is why the response to testosterone is lost.
Testosterone is slow because it must be carried across the membrane by a transport protein, and the drug blocks that carrier.
Steroids act as quickly as other hormones because they enter the cell directly, so the 30-minute delay must be an artefact of the experiment.
mcqs.specStatementText: Steroid hormones enter the cell and switch on genes
mcqs.explain: Dependence on transcription and a delay of minutes are the signature of a steroid hormone changing gene expression via an activated receptor; a response in seconds that survives transcription block shows epinephrine altering existing proteins via cAMP.
rationales: Dependence on transcription and a delay of minutes are the signature of a steroid hormone changing gene expression via an activated receptor; a response in seconds that survives transcription block shows epinephrine altering existing proteins via cAMP.
A student who thinks the hormone binds DNA directly picks this. Testosterone binds its receptor, and the receptor binds DNA; the drug blocks transcription, not hormone binding.
A student who believes hydrophobic molecules cannot cross the bilayer picks this. Steroids diffuse through the membrane freely; the delay reflects the time needed for transcription and translation.

A student who expects entering the cell to make a hormone faster picks this. A response that depends on making new mRNA and protein necessarily takes minutes to hours; the delay is real and diagnostic.

mcqs.q: For most of the menstrual cycle, oestradiol reduces the secretion of GnRH by cells in the hypothalamus. Late in the follicular phase, when oestradiol has been at a high level for about two days, GnRH secretion increases sharply. What best explains these observations?
options: Oestradiol can only inhibit GnRH secretion, so the sharp increase must have been caused by a different hormone.
Oestradiol's effect on GnRH-secreting cells switches from inhibition at moderate levels to stimulation at high sustained levels.
The early reduction was a harmful side effect of oestradiol and the later increase is its beneficial action.
Negative feedback lowers GnRH, so the sharp rise means the feedback loop has simply been switched off, with no new effect of oestradiol.
mcqs.specStatementText: What oestradiol does in the hypothalamus and progesterone in the endometrium
mcqs.explain: Oestradiol exerts negative feedback on the hypothalamic GnRH-secreting cells at low to moderate concentrations and positive feedback once it is high and sustained; the switch drives the surge that triggers ovulation.
rationales: A student who treats negative feedback as oestradiol's only possible action picks this. The same hormone stimulates GnRH secretion when its level is high and sustained.

Oestradiol exerts negative feedback on the hypothalamic GnRH-secreting cells at low to moderate concentrations and positive feedback once it is high and sustained; the switch drives the surge that triggers ovulation.
A student who reads negative feedback as 'harmful' picks this. Both effects are normal regulation: the inhibition keeps hormone levels stable and the stimulation drives ovulation.

A student who equates negative feedback with 'lowering' and its absence with a rise picks this. Removing inhibition would allow a return to baseline; the sharp surge shows active stimulation, which is positive feedback.

mcqs.q: What is the effect of progesterone on the cells of the endometrium?
options: It causes the endometrium to break down and be shed, which is why menstruation happens while progesterone is being secreted.
It binds directly to the DNA of the endometrial cells and switches on the genes that cause growth of the lining.
It maintains and thickens the endometrium, making its glands secrete and increasing its blood supply for implantation.
It binds to receptors on the surface of endometrial cells and raises cAMP inside them, which makes the lining grow much thicker.
mcqs.specStatementText: What oestradiol does in the hypothalamus and progesterone in the endometrium
mcqs.explain: Progesterone acts on endometrial cells after ovulation to keep the lining thick, secretory and well supplied with blood so that an embryo can implant; a fall in progesterone leads to menstruation.
rationales: A student who attaches shedding to the hormone rather than to its withdrawal picks this. Progesterone maintains the endometrium; menstruation follows the fall in progesterone at the end of the cycle.
A student who omits the receptor picks this. Progesterone binds and activates an intracellular receptor, and it is the receptor that binds specific DNA sequences.
Progesterone acts on endometrial cells after ovulation to keep the lining thick, secretory and well supplied with blood so that an embryo can implant; a fall in progesterone leads to menstruation.
A student who places every receptor on the cell surface picks this. Progesterone is a steroid: it enters the cell and acts through an intracellular receptor that affects gene expression.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between negative feedback and positive feedback in the regulation of signalling pathways?
options: Negative feedback produces harmful effects in the body, whereas positive feedback produces beneficial effects.
Negative feedback lowers the level of a variable, whereas positive feedback raises the level of a variable.
Negative feedback is used in healthy regulation, whereas positive feedback occurs only when regulation has failed.
In negative feedback the response reduces the stimulus; in positive feedback the response increases it.
mcqs.specStatementText: Negative feedback opposes change; positive feedback amplifies it
mcqs.explain: Negative feedback counteracts change and keeps a variable near a set level, as when oestradiol inhibits GnRH secretion; positive feedback amplifies change and drives a process to completion, as with oxytocin during birth.
rationales: A student who carries the everyday value-judgement meaning of the words into biology picks this. The terms describe the direction of the effect on the stimulus, and both forms are normal regulation.
A student who maps negative onto 'decrease' picks this. Negative feedback opposes change in either direction, raising a variable that has fallen as readily as lowering one that has risen.
A student who has met positive feedback only as a vicious circle picks this. Positive feedback is a normal mechanism for driving processes such as ovulation and birth to completion.

Negative feedback counteracts change and keeps a variable near a set level, as when oestradiol inhibits GnRH secretion; positive feedback amplifies change and drives a process to completion, as with oxytocin during birth.

mcqs.q: During birth, stretching of the cervix stimulates secretion of oxytocin, which strengthens contractions of the uterus, which stretch the cervix further, until the baby is delivered. How should this regulation be described?
options: Positive feedback, because each response increases the stimulus that caused it until an end point is reached.
Negative feedback, because the outcome of the process is beneficial to both the mother and the baby.
Negative feedback, because the whole process is switched off once the baby has been delivered.
A failure of regulation, because positive feedback of this kind does not occur in any healthy process.
mcqs.specStatementText: Negative feedback opposes change; positive feedback amplifies it
mcqs.explain: The response (stronger contractions) amplifies the stimulus (stretching), so the loop drives the process to completion; delivery removes the stimulus and ends the loop.
rationales: The response (stronger contractions) amplifies the stimulus (stretching), so the loop drives the process to completion; delivery removes the stimulus and ends the loop.
A student who judges feedback by whether the outcome is good picks this. The type of feedback depends on whether the response increases or reduces the stimulus, not on its benefit.
A student who equates negative feedback with stopping picks this. The loop ends because delivery removes the stimulus; while it runs, each response increases the stimulus, which is positive feedback.
A student who knows positive feedback only as a runaway fault picks this. Birth is a normal process in which positive feedback is used deliberately to drive contractions to completion.

specSource: IB Diploma Programme Biology (guide first assessment 2025); topic C2.1 Chemical signalling

specStatements.text: Receptors are proteins that bind one specific ligand
Bacteria count themselves with a shared secreted signal
Four functional categories of animal signalling chemicals
Signalling chemicals are chemically diverse, and that is useful
Hormones act far away; neurotransmitters act next door
Surface receptors for ligands that stay out; internal receptors for ligands that get in
Receptor activation starts a chain of events inside the cell
Neurotransmitter receptors open channels and change the voltage
Some receptors pass the signal to a G protein
Epinephrine acts through a G protein and cAMP
Insulin's receptor phosphorylates itself, and glucose transporters arrive
Steroid hormones enter the cell and switch on genes
What oestradiol does in the hypothalamus and progesterone in the endometrium

scopeNotes.howHonoured: The insulin pathway is described only as: insulin binds the receptor outside the cell, tyrosine residues on the receptor's cytoplasmic domain are phosphorylated, a sequence of reactions follows, and vesicles carrying glucose transporters move to and fuse with the plasma membrane. No intermediate proteins of the cascade (insulin receptor substrates, kinases such as PI3K or Akt) are named, and the transporter is referred to only as a glucose transporter.

Oestradiol's effects are tested only on the GnRH-secreting cells of the hypothalamus (inhibition at moderate concentrations, stimulation at high sustained concentrations). Progesterone's effects are tested only on cells of the endometrium. Effects of either hormone on the pituitary, ovary, breast, bone or other tissues are not included, and the full menstrual cycle is not taught here.

Feedback is tested only as the difference between negative feedback (the response counteracts the stimulus) and positive feedback (the response amplifies the stimulus), each illustrated briefly: oestradiol inhibiting GnRH secretion (negative) and oxytocin during birth (positive). The switch of oestradiol to stimulation of GnRH secretion, required by C2.1.13, is also labelled as positive feedback where it appears (c29, m30, m34) but is not used as a separate tested example. No quantitative treatment of feedback is included.

omitted.sequence: no authored ordering; would require inventing a sequence
